summary:
What if farmers could plan beyond their next harvest?

AgroSphere AI is a farm-planning platform that combines NASA Earth observation data with farmer inputs and transparent agronomic models. It helps farmers register a farm, examine historical environmental conditions, compare multi-season crop rotations, calculate water requirements, test hypothetical rainfall changes, review financial trade-offs, and save an evidence-backed plan.

The platform uses NASA POWER for historical temperature and precipitation, with location-gated processing paths for GPM IMERG precipitation, SMAP surface moisture, and HLS vegetation context. Environmental observations remain separate from farmer-entered soil tests and synthetic demonstration data.

Every result identifies its sources, assumptions, coverage, and limitations. Rainfall scenarios are clearly labelled as hypothetical rather than forecasts, and regional satellite observations are not presented as exact field measurements.

Designed initially for Sri Lankan farming conditions, AgroSphere AI demonstrates how accessible Earth intelligence can support more resilient and informed crop-rotation decisions.
details:
AgroSphere AI is an integrated decision-support platform for climate-resilient crop-rotation planning. It connects historical NASA Earth observations, farmer-provided farm information, transparent agronomic calculations, climate scenarios, financial comparisons, and grounded explanations in one workflow.

HOW IT WORKS

A farmer begins by registering a farm location, land area, crop history, irrigation information, priorities, exclusions, and any available soil-test results. Unknown values remain explicitly unknown instead of being silently converted to zero.

The platform retrieves and preserves historical NASA POWER observations for the selected location and period. These include daily precipitation and temperature with their dates, units, spatial context, coverage, retrieval metadata, and missing-value information. NASA observations are stored as immutable snapshots so later analyses remain reproducible.

AgroSphere AI then compares possible multi-season crop rotations. The rotation engine evaluates crop-family repetition, crop diversity, seasonal water demand, climate suitability, farmer constraints, and potential soil-management benefits. It calculates transparent water budgets using historical rainfall, crop demand, and known field-applied irrigation. Results are screening comparisons rather than guaranteed yield or planting prescriptions.

Farmers can create hypothetical rainfall-change scenarios from an existing analysis. For example, they can test how a rotation might respond if rainfall were 30% lower. The original NASA observation is never modified. The platform creates a separate scenario snapshot, recalculates the affected water and resilience indicators, and clearly labels the result as a hypothetical sensitivity analysis rather than a weather forecast.

The application also provides location-gated processing and presentation paths for GPM IMERG precipitation, SMAP regional surface-moisture context, and HLS vegetation-index context. These products remain separate from field soil tests and the NASA POWER rainfall baseline. SMAP is not converted into exact root-zone water, nutrients, or soil-health scores. HLS NDVI is not presented as a weed, species, nutrient, or yield detector.

A grounded assistant explains the selected farm, observation, analysis, scenario, and crop-rotation candidate. Its answers preserve source identifiers, assumptions, and limitations. The backend currently supports English and safely returns an explicit unsupported-language response for other languages instead of inventing an answer. The interface includes English, Sinhala, and Tamil resources.

Farmers can save immutable plan snapshots containing the farm, observation, analysis, scenario, and chosen candidate. Saved plans support reports, JSON export, printing, offline viewing, an action calendar, and farmer-entered season feedback. Feedback remains separate from NASA observations and does not silently retrain the model.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

AgroSphere AI turns complex Earth observation data into an understandable planning journey. It helps farmers compare alternatives across several seasons, examine water and climate trade-offs, preserve the evidence behind a decision, and understand uncertainty. Beginning with Sri Lanka, the platform is designed so its location, crop catalog, and agronomic rules can be adapted for other regions.

TRANSPARENCY AND SAFETY

The platform distinguishes NASA-derived observations, researched agronomic values, farmer-entered measurements, modeled estimates, hypothetical scenarios, and synthetic demonstrations. It never substitutes synthetic values when a live NASA product is unavailable. Regional satellite data is not described as an on-farm measurement, historical information is not presented as a forecast, and crop recommendations remain subject to local agronomic review.

TECHNOLOGY

The frontend was developed with React, TypeScript, Vite, React Router, TanStack Query, Zustand, i18next, Recharts, Leaflet, and OpenStreetMap. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, and provider-specific NASA data services. The system is deployed using Vercel and Render, with PostgreSQL persistence. Automated Python and frontend tests validate data contracts, calculations, APIs, error states, and interface behaviour.

The source code and technical documentation are publicly available at:

https://github.com/mbimsara/NASA-Space-App

CREATIVITY

The project’s main innovation is not simply displaying satellite data. Every capability shares the same versioned farm context and contributes to one explainable crop-rotation decision. Historical observations, rotation alternatives, water budgets, hypothetical climate stress, financial inputs, explanations, and saved plans remain connected while retaining their individual provenance and limitations.
